questions.explanation: The combination of a tall stature, signs of androgen deficiency (scant hair, small genitalia), and the pathognomonic 47, XXY karyotype is diagnostic of Klinefelter's syndrome (Option B). This is the most common cause of primary hypogonadism in males. The elevated LH and FSH levels occur due to the lack of negative feedback from the failing testes (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). Vanishing testis syndrome (Option A) would result in a similar hormonal profile but would lack the specific XXY genetics and tall stature. Noonan syndrome (Option C) presents with characteristic facial features and heart defects, usually with a 46, XY karyotype. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Option D) typically presents with ambiguous genitalia in females or precocious puberty in males. Therefore, the specific chromosomal finding of XXY confirms Klinefelter's syndrome as the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman who has recently delivered a baby wishes to avoid pregnancy for the next three years. Which contraceptive method would be the most suitable choice for her?
questions.explanation: For a postpartum woman seeking reliable, long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) for a duration of three years, the progesterone-releasing Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD), such as Mirena, is the most appropriate choice (Option B). These devices are safe for breast feeding mothers as they do not contain estrogen, which can interfere with milk production. They offer high efficacy and can remain in place for up to 5–8 years, covering the patient's three-year goal easily. The barrier method (Option A) has a higher failure rate and is less convenient for long-term use. Injectable progesterone (Option C) requires dosing every 3 months, making it less "long-acting" and reliable than an IUD. Lactational amenorrhea (Option D) is only reliable for the first six months postpartum if exclusive breastfeeding is practiced. Therefore, the IUCD provides the best balance of safety, duration, and efficacy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman (P1L1) with one living child is planning to conceive again and has been newly diagnosed with Graves’ disease. Which antithyroid drug is preferred for use during early pregnancy?
questions.explanation: For women with hyperthyroidism planning a pregnancy, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the drug of choice during the early gestation (first trimester) (Option A). PTU is preferred because it is more highly protein-bound and crosses the placenta less readily than other options, and most importantly, it is not associated with the specific "methimazole embryopathy". Methimazole (Option B) and its prodrug Carbimazole (Option C) are associated with rare but severe congenital defects such as aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, and esophageal atresia when used in early pregnancy. Many protocols involve switching the patient to PTU for the first trimester and then back to Methimazole for the remainder of the pregnancy to minimize PTU-related maternal hepatotoxicity. Therefore, to protect the fetus during organogenesis, PTU is the definitive standard recommendation for early pregnancy management of Graves' disease

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment option for an 8 cm endometrial cyst?
questions.explanation: An 8 cm endometrial cyst (endometrioma or "chocolate cyst") is a large lesion that warrants active surgical intervention. The most appropriate and standard treatment is surgical cystectomy (Option B), usually performed laparoscopically. Cystectomy involves excising the cyst wall, which provides higher relief of symptoms and a lower rate of recurrence compared to other methods. Needle aspiration (Option A) carries an extremely high risk of recurrence and potential spillage of irritant contents, making it less preferred. Medical management with GnRH agonists (Option C) can shrink the cyst temporarily and improve pelvic pain but will not resolve a large 8 cm collection. Conservative management (Option D) is generally only for very small ( cm) cysts; a large 8 cm cyst is at high risk for ovarian torsion or rupture. Therefore, laparoscopic excision is the definitive clinical standard

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms is the causative agent most commonly associated with acne fulminans?
questions.explanation: Acne fulminans is a rare and severe immunological reaction that represents the most extreme form of acne vulgaris. It is triggered by an abnormal systemic immune response to the antigens of Propionibacterium acnes (now renamed Cutibacterium acnes) (Option B). This bacterium is a normal inhabitant of the pilosebaceous unit. In acne fulminans, the body reacts with high levels of inflammation, leading to painful, ulcerated acne lesions and systemic symptoms like fever and bone pain. Actinomyces (Option A) causes actinomycosis, typically presenting with sulfur granules in jaw abscesses. Mobiluncus (Option C) is associated with bacterial vaginosis. Bifidobacterium (Option D) is a common gut probiotic and not a primary skin pathogen. Therefore, the hypersensitivity reaction to P. acnes is the definitive underlying cause of this severe dermatological condition. Management usually requires systemic corticosteroids and isotretinoin

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents to the dermatology outpatient department with the skin condition shown. Based on her pregnancy status and the clinical appearance, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows blotchy, brownish hyperpigmentation on the cheeks and forehead of a pregnant woman, which is the pathognomonic presentation of Chloasma (Option D). Also known as melasma or the "mask of pregnancy," it is a common physiological skin change occurring in up to 70% of pregnant women. It is caused by the stimulatory effect of pregnancy hormones (estrogen, progesterone, and MSH) on melanocytes, exacerbated by sun exposure. Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A) presents with a "malar rash" that is typically erythematous and spares the nasolabial folds, unlike the brown pigmentation seen here. Viral infections (Option B) and rosacea (Option C) would present with redness, pustules, or systemic symptoms rather than isolated pigmentation. Therefore, chloasma is the most probable diagnosis. It is benign and usually fades after delivery as hormone levels normalize

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following does not exhibit the Koebner's phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Koebner’s phenomenon, also known as the "isomorphic response," refers to the development of new skin lesions typical of a pre-existing dermatosis at sites of local trauma or injury. Classic examples of skin diseases that exhibit this phenomenon include Vitiligo (Option A), Psoriasis (Option B), and Lichen planus (Option C). Herpes (Option D) is a viral infection; while trauma can reactivate a latent virus (triggering a cold sore), it does not follow the definitive clinical definition of Koebner’s phenomenon, which specifically describes the linear induction of chronic dermatoses by trauma. Other conditions showing Koebner’s include warts and molluscum contagiosum (due to autoinoculation). Because Herpes is an acute, localized viral process rather than a trauma-induced distribution of a chronic dermatosis, it is the correct "not" choice. Recognizing this phenomenon is useful for clinicians when assessing the distribution of lesions

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the type of psoriasis in the given picture.
questions.explanation: The image shows multiple small, drop-like erythematous papules with fine scaling scattered over the skin. This pattern is characteristic of guttate psoriasis. The term “guttate” comes from the Latin word gutta, meaning “drop,” reflecting the raindrop-like lesions. Guttate psoriasis commonly: 1. Affects children and young adults 2. Appears suddenly, often after a streptococcal infection 3. Involves the trunk and proximal limbs 4. Shows numerous small lesions, unlike large plaques Why other options are incorrect: (B) Erythrodermic psoriasis → Diffuse redness involving almost entire body (C) Pustular psoriasis → Presence of pus-filled lesions, not seen here (D) Inverse psoriasis → Occurs in skin folds, smooth and shiny lesions without scaling

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with a chronic skin lesion that has a rough, scaly surface. Skin biopsy shows marked hyperkeratosis. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of a scaly, rough skin lesion in a young adult is highly suggestive of Psoriasis (Option B). The histopathological finding of marked hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum) is a classic feature of psoriasis, along with parakeratosis and acanthosis. Atopic dermatitis (Option A) typically presents as itchy, poorly defined eczematous patches in the flexures, often with a different histological pattern. Pemphigus vulgaris (Option C) and Pemphigus foliaceus (Option D) are autoimmune blistering diseases; they present with fluid-filled vesicles or erosions rather than primary thick scaly plaques. Pemphigus vulgaris specifically involves painful mucosal erosions and deep blisters. Therefore, the specific combination of a chronic scaly plaque and hyperkeratosis on biopsy makes psoriasis the most probable and accurate diagnosis. Psoriasis lesions are typically well-demarcated with silvery scales

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman with diabetes and a history of recurrent deep vein thrombosis, currently receiving anticoagulant therapy, presents with a rapidly progressive skin lesion. What began as a small lesion has quickly enlarged to involve the entire limb and abdomen. Based on the clinical history and the image provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: (Note: There is a significant discrepancy between the clinical description of a "rapidly enlarging skin lesion" and the provided options, which are all pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. However, based on the classic "skin-tumor" association in medical exams...). The diagnosis is Glucagonoma (Option C). This rare tumor secretes excessive glucagon, which leads to a pathognomonic skin condition known as Necrolytic Migratory Erythema (NME). NME typically presents as an enlarging, painful rash with central clearing and necrosis that "migrates" or spreads across the abdomen and limbs. The patient’s history of DVT is also a classic component of the glucagonoma syndrome. Insulinoma (Option A) causes hypoglycemia. Gastrinoma (Option B) causes severe peptic ulcers. VIPoma (Option D) causes profuse watery diarrhea. Therefore, despite the vague description, the specific association between an extensive spreading skin lesion, DVT, and these neuroendocrine options confirms Glucagonoma as the intended answer

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a markedly swollen foot associated with multiple discharging sinuses, as shown in the provided image. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the classic clinical triad for Mycetoma (Madura foot): localized swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and the discharge of purulent fluid containing granules. Mycetoma is a chronic granulomatous infection typically contracted by farmers who work barefoot and sustain minor trauma from thorns or soil. It can be caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or bacteria (actinomycetoma). Squamous cell carcinoma (Option B) presents as a non-healing ulcer but not with multiple sinuses and granules. Nocardia (Option C) is a cause of actinomycetoma but the overall "condition" is termed Mycetoma. Sporotrichosis (Option D) usually follows a "lymphocutaneous" pattern with nodules along the lymphatic channels rather than a massive localized foot swelling. Therefore, the characteristic physical appearance of the sinuses and swelling in a rural worker confirms Mycetoma as the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What are the standard preoperative fasting recommendations for different patient categories to reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration during anesthesia?
options: 2 hours for breast milk in infants
questions.explanation: According to the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) guidelines, standardized NPO (nothing by mouth) times are mandated to ensure gastric emptying before anesthesia. The correct recommendation is 2 hours for clear liquids in adults (Option B). This applies to water, fruit juices without pulp, and clear tea. Option A is incorrect because 6 to 8 hours is the required time for solids in adults. For infants, the specific rules are: 4 hours for breast milk (Option C is incorrect as it says 2 hours) and 6 hours for infant formula or solids (Option D is incorrect). These protocols are strictly enforced to prevent the life-threatening complication of Mendelson's syndrome (aspiration of gastric contents). Therefore, the 2-hour window for clear liquids is the only accurately stated guideline among the choices provided

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: While observing anesthesia equipment in the operating theater, a specific vaporizer is in use. Which of the following gases is it most likely designed to contain?
questions.explanation: Anesthesia equipment uses a universal color-coding system to prevent medication errors. A vaporizer with a blue color-coded dial or housing is designed exclusively for Desflurane (Option A). Desflurane requires a specialized heated and pressurized vaporizer (like the Tec 6) due to its extremely high vapor pressure and boiling point near room temperature. Halothane (Option B) is color-coded red. Sevoflurane (Option C) is color-coded yellow. Isoflurane (Option D) is color-coded purple. Identifying these colors is a fundamental safety skill for anesthetists. Since the vaporizer in the image is marked with the blue distinctive color of Desflurane, that is the gas it comprises. This visual identification ensures that the correct agent is matched to its corresponding calibrated delivery device

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following beta blockers has a short duration of action?
questions.explanation: Esmolol (Option C) is an ultra-short-acting cardioselective beta-1 antagonist with a half-life of only 9 minutes. It is rapidly hydrolyzed by red blood cell esterases, which allows for very precise titration when given intravenously. This makes it the drug of choice for managing acute perioperative hypertension or tachycardia. Nadolol (Option A) is a long-acting beta-blocker with a half-life of 20–24 hours, requiring only once-daily dosing. Propranolol (Option B) is a non-selective agent with an intermediate duration of 3–6 hours. Atenolol (Option D) is also an intermediate-to-long-acting cardioselective agent. Because Esmolol's effects are almost immediately reversible by stopping the infusion, it provides a unique safety advantage in unstable patients. Therefore, Esmolol is the definitive answer for the shortest-acting beta-blocker

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a gradually enlarging swelling near the wrist joint over the past three months. Based on the X-ray findings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays an expansile, multi-loculated lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, classically described as having a "soap-bubble" appearance. The lesion extends right up to the subchondral bone (articular surface). These are pathognomonic radiological features of Osteoclastoma, also known as a Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) (Option C). GCT is typically seen in young adults (ages 20–40) and is locally aggressive. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option A) presents with an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction in the diaphysis of long bones. Osteosarcoma (Option B) would show a "sunburst" periosteal reaction and a Codman’s triangle. Osteochondroma (Option D) appears as a bony outgrowth on a stalk (exostosis). Therefore, the subarticular location and soap-bubble morphology confirm Osteoclastoma as the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old man reports progressive low back pain and morning stiffness for the past six months, with relief on physical activity. He also has a known history of ulcerative colitis. Based on the X-ray of the lumbar spine shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of chronic inflammatory back pain (worse in the morning, improves with exercise) and a history of inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) is highly suggestive of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. The provided X-ray provides the definitive diagnosis, showing vertical syndesmophytes fusing the vertebral bodies, creating the classic "bamboo spine" appearance of Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option C). Pott’s spine (Option A) is spinal tuberculosis, which causes vertebral destruction and angulation (gibbus) rather than smooth fusion. Psoriatic arthritis (Option B) can cause sacroiliitis but usually presents with asymmetric large syndesmophytes. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D) primarily affects the small joints of the hands and the cervical spine, not the lumbar spine in this manner. Therefore, the pathognomonic "bamboo spine" in the context of IBD confirms Ankylosing Spondylitis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis made from the MRI image given below?
questions.explanation: The MRI image reveals destruction of adjacent vertebral bodies and the intervening disc space, accompanied by a large prevertebral and paravertebral fluid collection. This is the hallmark of Pott’s spine (Spinal Tuberculosis). The fluid collection is known as a "cold abscess" because it lacks the intense acute inflammation of a pyogenic infection. Multiple myeloma (Option A) causes multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions but usually spares the disc space. Ankylosing spondylitis (Option B) shows fusion and syndesmophytes without abscess formation. Pyogenic spondylitis (Option C) presents with more acute, rapid bone destruction and systemic toxicity compared to the subacute nature of TB. Because Pott’s spine characteristically involves two adjacent vertebrae, destroys the disc, and forms large paravertebral abscesses, it is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old man reports progressive low back pain and morning stiffness for the past six months, with relief on physical activity. He also has a known history of ulcerative colitis. Based on the X-ray of the lumbar spine shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray displays numerous well-circumscribed, "punched-out," and widely scattered round opacities in both lungs. These are known as "cannonball metastases" (Option C). In an elderly male with weight loss and anemia, these likely represent spread from a primary malignancy such as renal cell carcinoma or colorectal cancer. Bronchogenic carcinoma (Option A) typically presents as a single large hilar mass or a peripheral nodule. Mesothelioma (Option B) involves diffuse pleural thickening rather than parenchymal balls. Pneumoconiosis (Option D) involves much smaller, diffuse, and poorly defined nodules related to occupational dust inhalation. Therefore, the characteristic large, discrete, and bilateral "cannonball" appearance is definitive for secondary metastatic deposits. This radiographic finding is a classic clinical indicator of late-stage systemic malignancy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man’s chest X-ray shows bilateral blunting of the costophrenic angles along with a meniscus sign on the lateral view. Which condition is most consistent with these radiographic findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical hallmarks of a Pleural Effusion on a chest radiograph are the blunting of the costophrenic angle (where the lung meets the diaphragm) and the meniscus sign. The meniscus sign is a concave upper border of the fluid, created by the fluid climbing higher at the periphery due to capillary action and negative intrathoracic pressure. Emphysema (Option A) would show hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms. Tension pneumothorax (Option B) would show a dark, air-filled pleural space without lung markings and a shifted mediastinum. Bronchiectasis (Option D) typically shows "tram-track" opacities or cystic changes, not localized fluid collection in the base. Therefore, the specific combination of angle blunting and a radiographic meniscus is definitive for fluid in the pleural cavity. Bilateral involvement in a 65-year-old often suggests a systemic cause like congestive heart failure

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident with acute respiratory distress and distended neck veins. Imaging shows a large collection of air on the left side of the chest. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of trauma, respiratory distress, dilated neck veins (elevated JVP), and an X-ray showing a large volume of air in the hemithorax is pathognomonic for a Tension Pneumothorax. This is a life-threatening emergency where air under pressure compresses the heart and the opposite lung. The most appropriate immediate management is needle decompression. According to modern ATLS guidelines, this is performed by inserting a wide-bore needle into the 5th intercostal space in the mid-axillary line (or the 2nd space mid-clavicular line). This converts the tension pneumothorax into a simple one, stabilizing the patient until a chest tube can be placed. Intubation (Option B) and tracheostomy (Option C) address airway obstruction, not pleural air. Pericardiocentesis (Option D) is for cardiac tamponade. Therefore, immediate decompression is the life-saving next step

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the underlying condition as shown in the below radiograp
questions.explanation: The radiograph of the newborn suggests imperforate anus, a congenital anomaly in which the anal opening is absent or obstructed, preventing the normal passage of stool. Imperforate anus is part of a spectrum of anorectal malformations, which vary in severity and complexity. It occurs in approximately 1 in 5,000 live births and can affect both males and females. On the radiograph, there is an absence of gas in the rectum and sigmoid colon, indicating distal bowel obstruction. The presence of abdominal distension further supports this diagnosis, as accumulation of intestinal contents leads to swelling of the abdomen. Reasons for excluding other options : Meningocele is a neural tube defect involving herniation of meninges and is not identified on an abdominal radiograph. Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung’s disease) causes bowel obstruction but typically shows gas patterns extending to the colon and does not involve absence of the anal opening. Pyloric stenosis leads to vomiting due to gastric outlet obstruction and does not affect the distal bowel or rectal gas pattern

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the investigation performed in the condition shown below in the radiograph?
options: Retrograde cystourethrogram with membranous urethra stricture
Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture
Micturating cystourethrography with psoriatic urethra stricture
questions.explanation: (Note: There is a minor anatomical discrepancy between the image provided and the options, as most strictures pictured in this set are bulbar. However, based on the options provided for this specific question...). The image shows a Retrograde Cystourethrogram (RGU), identified by the contrast being injected "upward" from the tip of the penis to visualize the urethra. This is the standard investigation for suspected urethral strictures. The image reveals a narrow, diseased segment of the penile (anterior) urethra. A Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) (Options C and D) is performed while the patient is voiding to visualize the posterior urethra and bladder neck. Membranous strictures (Option A) occur higher up at the level of the pelvic floor and are usually traumatic. There is no such thing as a "psoriatic" stricture (Option D). Therefore, based on the retrograde injection method and the location of the narrowing, RGU of a penile stricture is the correct identification

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use and smoking presents with repeated episodes of vomiting and sudden, sharp epigastric pain. The symptoms began shortly after heavy alcohol intake. He is now febrile and tachycardic. Bedside imaging reveals the presence of free air under the diaphragm. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with recurrent vomiting and sudden sharp epigastric pain, along with a history of chronic alcohol consumption and smoking, which are strong risk factors for peptic ulcer disease (PUD). The X-ray shows a key diagnostic feature: free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). This indicates perforation of a hollow viscus, most commonly due to a perforated peptic ulcer. When an ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the stomach or duodenal wall, air escapes into the peritoneal cavity, producing this classic radiological sign. Clinically, perforation presents with: 1. Sudden severe epigastric pain (“stabbing”) 2. Vomiting 3. Signs of peritonitis (guarding, rigidity) 4. Possible fever and tachycardia Why other options are incorrect: 1. Tension pneumothorax → Chest findings, not abdominal free air 2. Boerhaave syndrome → Esophageal rupture, shows mediastinal air 3. Mallory-Weiss tear → Causes bleeding, not perforation

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with recurrent frontal headaches, prompting evaluation of the paranasal sinuses. Which radiographic view is best suited for optimal visualization of the frontal sinuses to assess for sinusitis?
questions.explanation: To evaluate the paranasal sinuses via conventional radiography, specific views are used for different anatomical areas. The Caldwell view (posteroanterior with a 15-degree downward tilt) is the most effective and standard view for detailed visualization of the frontal sinuses (Option B). It also provides good views of the ethmoid sinuses. Waters view (Option C) is the gold standard specifically for the maxillary sinuses. The lateral view (Option A) is useful for the sphenoid sinus and seeing the depth of the frontal sinus but provides poor overall detail compared to the frontal projections. The Submentovertex view (Option D) is primarily used for the skull base and zygomatic arches. Therefore, because the patient’s clinical concern is frontal sinusitis, the Caldwell view is the definitive radiological choice to clear that specific area. It allows the sinuses to be projected above the petrous ridges

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An elderly woman presents with mptoms of confusion, intense thirst, abdominal discomfort, a pale complexion, and sensitivity in her thoracic spine. Her lab results show signincant findings: 1. Hemoglobin (Hb) : 6.9 g/ dL 2. White Blood Cell count : rBq c m 40 0 3 ο , 3. With a normal differential 4. Serum calcium: 13 mg/dL 5. Creatinine: 2.3 mg/dl 6. Albumin: 2.4 g/dl 7. Urinalysis: Positive for Bence-lones proteins 8. A skull X-ray indicates lytic lesions. Based on 9. These findings, what is the most likely diaglosis?
questions.explanation: The provided image and clinical triad are pathognomonic for Multiple Myeloma (Option B). This is a plasma cell malignancy characterized by the "CRAB" features: Calcium elevation (13 mg/dL), Renal insufficiency (Creatinine 2.3), Anemia (Hb 6.9), and Bone lesions. The presence of Bence-Jones proteins (monoclonal light chains) in the urine is a specific diagnostic hallmark. The skull X-ray provides definitive visual confirmation, showing multiple, small, well-defined "punched-out" lytic lesions. Metastatic breast cancer (Option A) can cause lytic lesions but would not show Bence-Jones proteins. Primary hyperparathyroidism (Option C) causes hypercalcemia and a "salt and pepper" skull but lacks monoclonal proteins. Milk-alkali syndrome (Option D) involves hypercalcemia without skeletal destruction. Therefore, the combination of specific laboratory markers and pathognomonic radiographic findings confirms Multiple Myeloma as the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A neonate presents with features of congestive heart failure. On examination, there is an enlarged fontanelle and a bruit is heard on auscultation. Ultrasound reveals a midline hypoechoic lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a neonate with high-output congestive heart failure, enlarging fontanelles (hydrocephalus), and a cranial bruit heard on auscultation is pathognomonic for a Vein of Galen Malformation (VOGM) (Option A). VOGM is a direct arteriovenous shunting from cerebral arteries into the great cerebral vein, which dilates into a massive aneurysmal sac. The USG midline hypoechoic lesion represents this dilated venous sac. Aqueduct stenosis (Option B) and arachnoid cysts (Option C) cause hydrocephalus but would not cause heart failure or a bruit. Medulloblastoma (Option D) is a malignant posterior fossa tumor that typically presents in older children, not as a neonate in heart failure. The shunt in VOGM acts as a low-resistance path for blood, forcing the heart to work excessively to maintain systemic circulation. Therefore, VOGM is the only diagnosis that accounts for both the neurological and cardiovascular findings

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with loss of consciousness. A CT scan shows multiple small, spotty hemorrhages with preserved (full) basal cisterns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In the setting of a high-speed road traffic accident followed by immediate coma, Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) is a leading diagnosis (Option B). DAI is caused by shear forces that tear axons throughout the brain. The hallmark CT findings are multiple spotty (petechial) hemorrhages, typically located at the grey-white matter junction, in the corpus callosum, or in the brainstem. Brain contusions (Option A) are "bruises" typically found at the impact site (coup) or opposite site (contre-coup). A subdural hematoma (Option C) would appear as a crescent-shaped blood collection. Multiple infarcts (Option D) involve ischemic strokes and would not be the primary result of acute trauma. While CT may appear relatively "normal" compared to the patient's severe clinical state, the presence of these spotty hemorrhages in a comatose patient is highly diagnostic. Therefore, DAI represents the severe widespread traumatic injury described by these specific radiological cues

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 39-year- old man who repeatedly washes his hands 15–20 times daily due to persistent fears of contamination, resulting in significant impairment in his occupational functioning?
questions.explanation: The patient’s behavior fulfills the core diagnostic criteria for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) (Option B). OCD is characterized by the presence of obsessions (intrusive, persistent thoughts of contamination) and compulsions (repetitive behaviors like excessive hand washing) aimed at reducing the distress caused by the obsessions. These symptoms are time-consuming and lead to significant impairment in social or occupational functioning. Bipolar disorder (Option A) involves cycles of depression and mania, while Mania (Option D) is characterized by elevated mood and racing thoughts, not contamination obsessions. Schizophrenia (Option C) involves hallucinations and delusions. Because the patient's symptoms are specifically centered on a contamination ritual that he feels compelled to perform to neutralize his anxiety, OCD is the definitive psychiatric diagnosis. Management typically involves selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and cognitive-behavioral therapy

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A young man with a paternal family history of bipolar disorder presents to the OPD with three documented manic episodes. Which mood stabilizer would be the most appropriate and effective treatment option for him?
questions.explanation: For a patient with recurrent episodes of classic mania and a strong family history of the disorder, Lithium remains the "gold standard" mood stabilizer (Option D). Lithium is highly effective at both treating acute manic episodes and preventing future recurrences of mania and depression. Valproate (Option A) is an excellent alternative, particularly for "mixed episodes" or rapid cycling, but Lithium is classically favored for pure manic presentations. Lamotrigine (Option B) is primarily effective for the maintenance phase of bipolar depression rather than acute mania. Olanzapine (Option C) is an atypical antipsychotic used for acute stabilization but is not the primary long-term mood stabilizer compared to the established efficacy of lithium. Therefore, given the specific recurrent manic history, Lithium is the most appropriate and historically validated choice for this patient. Monitoring of serum lithium levels and renal/thyroid function is mandatory

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In a clinical evaluation, a patient reports deriving sexual gratification from inflicting physical injury on their partner, leading to cuts and burns. What term most accurately describes this behavior?
questions.explanation: The behavior described is a paraphilic disorder known as Sexual Sadism (Option C). It involves deriving sexual excitement and pleasure from the infliction of physical or psychological suffering, pain, or humiliation on another person. Masochism (Option D) is the opposite, where an individual derives pleasure from receiving pain or humiliation. Voyeurism (Option A) involves sexual arousal from observing unsuspecting people who are naked or engaging in sexual activity. Fetishism (Option B) involves sexual arousal from non-living objects or specific non-genital body parts. Because the patient's arousal is specifically linked to the active causing of harm (cuts and burns) to a partner, it fits the definitive clinical definition of sadism. This behavior can be part of a consensual relationship or can cross into criminal assault depending on the context and consent

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In a 70-year-old patient with schizophrenia who is being treated for drug-induced Parkinsonism, which medication is most likely responsible for anticholinergic side effects such as constipation, blurred vision, and dry mouth?
questions.explanation: Drug-induced Parkinsonism is a common side effect of traditional antipsychotic medications used for schizophrenia. To manage these motor symptoms, clinicians often prescribe anticholinergic medications like Benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl) (Option C). These drugs block acetylcholine to restore the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia. However, they cause significant systemic anticholinergic side effects, including dry mouth (xerostomia), blurred vision (due to mydriasis/cycloplegia), and constipation. Lithium (Option A) causes polyuria and tremors. Pramipexole (Option B), a dopamine agonist, causes nausea and orthostatic hypotension. Selegiline (Option D), an MAO-B inhibitor, is less associated with this classic anticholinergic triad. Therefore, given the specific combination of symptoms—dry mouth, constipation, and blurred vision—Benzhexol is the definitive medication responsible for the patient's distress. These side effects are particularly bothersome in elderly patients and can exacerbate pre-existing glaucoma or urinary retention. **************
